title: 2 Peter COMA Study
description: 3-week walkthrough of 2 Peter using the COMA method (Context, Observation, Meaning, Application) from a Reformed Baptist perspective

subsections.title: Introduction to 2 Peter
subsections.content:
The apostle Peter wrote this letter near the end of his life (around AD 64-68), knowing his death was imminent (2 Peter 1:14). He writes to the same audience as his first letter—believers scattered throughout Asia Minor—but now addresses a different threat: false teachers who deny the Lord and lead others into destructive heresies.

The letter's major themes include: the precious promises that enable us to escape corruption, the importance of growing in godly virtues, the certainty of Christ's return despite scoffers' mockery, and the danger of false teaching. Peter emphasizes knowledge throughout—true knowledge of God and Christ versus the deceptive 'knowledge' of the false teachers.

This week we explore Peter's greeting and his call to confirm our calling through spiritual growth.

subsections.title: Greeting
subsections.content: Peter identifies himself and blesses his readers.

questions.question: Context: How does Peter identify himself (2 Peter 1:1)? Why might he emphasize being both 'a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ'?
Observation: How did the recipients obtain their faith (2 Peter 1:1)? What does Peter wish for them (2 Peter 1:2)? How is this obtained?

Meaning: What does 'a faith of equal standing with ours' (2 Peter 1:1) teach about the equality of all believers before God? What does it mean that this faith was 'obtained' through the righteousness of God and Jesus Christ? How does 'knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord' (2 Peter 1:2) multiply grace and peace?
Application: Do you view your faith as equally precious as that of the apostles? How can you grow in 'knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord'?

subsections.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
subsections.content: Peter describes the precious promises that enable us to escape worldly corruption.

questions.question: Context: How do these verses expand on the greeting's emphasis on 'knowledge'? What has divine power granted?

Observation: What has 'his divine power' granted us (2 Peter 1:3)? Through what knowledge? By what were we called (2 Peter 1:3)? What has God granted through these promises (2 Peter 1:4)? What do we escape?

Meaning: What does 'all things that pertain to life and godliness' (2 Peter 1:3) encompass? What does it mean to become 'partakers of the divine nature' (2 Peter 1:4)—is Peter teaching that we become divine? How does this relate to union with Christ and sanctification? What is 'the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire' (2 Peter 1:4)?
Application: Are you drawing on 'all things that pertain to life and godliness' that God has granted? What worldly corruption are you seeking to escape through God's promises?

subsections.title: Supplement Your Faith
subsections.content: Peter calls believers to add virtue upon virtue to their faith.

questions.question: Context: How does 'For this very reason' (2 Peter 1:5) connect to the previous promises? Why does effort follow from divine provision?

Observation: What eight qualities should believers 'supplement' or add to their faith (2 Peter 1:5-7)? What do these qualities produce (2 Peter 1:8)? What is true of one who lacks them (2 Peter 1:9)? What should believers do (2 Peter 1:10)? What is promised (2 Peter 1:10-11)?

Meaning: Why does the list begin with faith and end with love (2 Peter 1:5-7)? What does 'make every effort' (2 Peter 1:5) teach about the role of human effort in sanctification? How can someone have 'forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins' (2 Peter 1:9)? What does 'confirm your calling and election' (2 Peter 1:10) mean—can we lose our election, or is this about assurance? Note that election is God's sovereign choice; confirmation is our responsibility to demonstrate its reality.
Application: Which of the eight qualities do you most need to cultivate? How can you 'make every effort' while still depending on God's power? Are you confident of your calling and election?

subsections.title: Peter's Reminder and the Prophetic Word
subsections.content: Peter explains why he writes and points to the reliability of Scripture.

questions.question: Context: Why does Peter feel urgency in reminding them of these things (2 Peter 1:13-15)? What does he know about his future?

Observation: What did the apostles not follow (2 Peter 1:16)? What did they witness (2 Peter 1:16-18)? What do we have that is 'more fully confirmed' (2 Peter 1:19)? How did prophecy come about (2 Peter 1:20-21)?

Meaning: What were the 'cleverly devised myths' (2 Peter 1:16) that Peter contrasts with eyewitness testimony? How is the Transfiguration connected to 'the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ' (2 Peter 1:16)? Why is 'the prophetic word' even more fully confirmed than eyewitness experience (2 Peter 1:19)? What does 'no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation' (2 Peter 1:20) mean? How were prophets 'carried along by the Holy Spirit' (2 Peter 1:21)?

Application: How does the reliability of Scripture as God-breathed affect how you read and obey it? Are you 'paying attention' to the prophetic word as to 'a lamp shining in a dark place' (2 Peter 1:19)?

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: Peter now turns to the main threat facing his readers: false teachers who introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them. This chapter is one of the strongest condemnations of false teaching in Scripture. Peter draws on historical examples—fallen angels, Noah's flood, and Sodom and Gomorrah—to show that God knows how to rescue the godly while reserving the unrighteous for judgment.

subsections.title: False Prophets and Teachers
subsections.content: Peter warns of false teachers who will arise from within the community.

questions.question: Context: How does Peter's transition from the true prophets (2 Peter 1:21) to false prophets (2 Peter 2:1) highlight the contrast he's making?

Observation: Just as there were false prophets in Israel, what will arise among believers (2 Peter 2:1)? What will they 'secretly bring in' (2 Peter 2:1)? What will many follow (2 Peter 2:2)? What is their motivation (2 Peter 2:3)?

Meaning: What are 'destructive heresies' (2 Peter 2:1)? What does it mean that they 'deny the Master who bought them' (2 Peter 2:1)—how should we understand this in light of particular redemption? Options include: they profess to be bought but weren't truly, or Peter uses 'bought' in a broader covenant sense. Why is 'the way of truth' blasphemed because of false teachers (2 Peter 2:2)? What 'words' do they use to exploit people (2 Peter 2:3)?
Application: How can you recognize false teachers today? What 'destructive heresies' are prevalent in our time? How does this warning affect how you evaluate teaching?

subsections.title: Examples of Divine Judgment
subsections.content: Peter gives three historical examples showing God's pattern of judgment and rescue.

questions.question: Context: Why does Peter reach back to Old Testament examples? What is the 'if...then' logic of his argument?

Observation: What three examples of judgment does Peter give (2 Peter 2:4-6)? Who was rescued in each case (2 Peter 2:5, 7)? What was Lot's experience among the wicked (2 Peter 2:7-8)? What conclusion does Peter draw (2 Peter 2:9-10a)?

Meaning: What happened to the angels who sinned (2 Peter 2:4)? What does 'a herald of righteousness' (2 Peter 2:5) tell us about Noah's ministry? How was Lot 'righteous' (2 Peter 2:7-8) despite his failures recorded in Genesis? What does it mean that God 'knows how to rescue the godly from trials' (2 Peter 2:9)? What characterizes those under judgment—'those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority' (2 Peter 2:10)?

Application: How does God's pattern of rescuing the godly while judging the wicked encourage you? Like Lot, do you find yourself 'tormented' by the lawlessness around you, or have you grown comfortable with it?

subsections.title: The Character of False Teachers
subsections.content: Peter describes the boldness, corruption, and deceptive tactics of false teachers.

questions.question: Context: How does this detailed description help believers identify false teachers?

Observation: What are false teachers 'bold' enough to do (2 Peter 2:10-11)? What are they compared to (2 Peter 2:12)? What do they count as pleasure (2 Peter 2:13)? What characterizes their eyes (2 Peter 2:14)? Whose way have they followed (2 Peter 2:15-16)?

Meaning: Why is blaspheming 'the glorious ones' (2 Peter 2:10) significant—even angels don't do this (2 Peter 2:11)? What does the animal comparison teach about their nature (2 Peter 2:12)? Who was Balaam and why is he the prototype of the false teacher (2 Peter 2:15-16; cf. Numbers 22-24)?
Application: What warning signs from this passage can help you identify false teachers? How do you evaluate whether someone loves 'gain from wrongdoing' (2 Peter 2:15) rather than genuine ministry?

subsections.title: The Slavery of the False Teachers
subsections.content: Peter describes the emptiness of the false teachers' promises and the danger they pose.

questions.question: Context: How do the images of 'waterless springs' and 'mists driven by a storm' (2 Peter 2:17) summarize Peter's critique?

Observation: What do false teachers promise (2 Peter 2:19)? What are they themselves (2 Peter 2:19)? What is true of those who escape worldly defilement but become entangled again (2 Peter 2:20-21)? What proverbs does Peter use (2 Peter 2:22)?

Meaning: How can someone promise 'freedom' while being a 'slave of corruption' (2 Peter 2:19)? What does 'the last state has become worse for them than the first' (2 Peter 2:20) teach? Does this passage teach that true believers can lose their salvation, or is Peter describing those who were never truly regenerate? Note the dog and pig imagery (2 Peter 2:22)—they return to their true nature. What is 'the holy commandment' (2 Peter 2:21)?
Application: What false 'freedom' is the world offering today? How can you discern between genuine escape from corruption (through Christ) and temporary moral reform that doesn't last?

gospelData.title: Week 3: The Day of the Lord

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: Peter concludes his letter by addressing scoffers who mock the promise of Christ's return. He explains why the Lord 'delays'—not because of inability but because of patience toward sinners. The certainty of the Day of the Lord should produce holy living and eager expectation. Peter commends Paul's writings and closes with a call to grow in grace and knowledge.

subsections.title: Scoffers in the Last Days
subsections.content: Peter warns of those who mock the promise of Christ's return.

questions.question: Context: Why does Peter mention 'this is now the second letter' (2 Peter 3:1)? What is he trying to stir up in his readers (2 Peter 3:1)?

Observation: What will come in the last days (2 Peter 3:3)? What do scoffers say (2 Peter 3:4)? What do they deliberately overlook (2 Peter 3:5-6)? What is stored up for the present heavens and earth (2 Peter 3:7)?

Meaning: What is the scoffers' argument from 'uniformity'—'all things are continuing as they were from the beginning' (2 Peter 3:4)? Why is this argument wrong? How does the Flood demonstrate God's willingness to intervene in judgment (2 Peter 3:6)? What is the 'fire' reserved for the day of judgment (2 Peter 3:7)?
Application: Do you ever wonder why Christ hasn't returned yet? How does the scoffers' reasoning appear in modern thought—even among believers?

subsections.title: The Lord Is Patient
subsections.content: Peter explains why the Lord 'delays' His coming.

questions.question: Context: How does Peter's explanation counter the scoffers' mockery?

Observation: What must readers 'not overlook' (2 Peter 3:8)? Is the Lord 'slow' in keeping His promise (2 Peter 3:9)? What is He instead? What does He not wish (2 Peter 3:9)? How will the day of the Lord come (2 Peter 3:10)?

Meaning: What does 'with the Lord one day is as a thousand years' (2 Peter 3:8) teach about God's relationship to time? What is God's patience 'toward you' (2 Peter 3:9) aiming at? In light of Reformed theology, how do we understand 'not wishing that any should perish'—is 'any' referring to the elect whom God is patiently gathering? What does 'like a thief' (2 Peter 3:10) emphasize about Christ's return?
Application: How does God's patience toward sinners affect your evangelism and prayers for the lost? Are you living as if Christ could return 'like a thief' at any moment?

subsections.title: What Sort of People Ought You to Be?
subsections.content: Peter draws ethical implications from the certainty of the Day of the Lord.

questions.question: Context: How does 'Since all these things are thus to be dissolved' (2 Peter 3:11) provide the basis for Peter's exhortation?

Observation: What should believers be characterized by (2 Peter 3:11)? What should they be 'waiting for and hastening' (2 Peter 3:12)? What do we await 'according to his promise' (2 Peter 3:13)? How should believers be found when Christ returns (2 Peter 3:14)?

Meaning: How can we 'hasten' the coming of the day of God (2 Peter 3:12)—through holy living, evangelism, or both? What are 'new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells' (2 Peter 3:13)? Why does Peter emphasize being found 'without spot or blemish, and at peace' (2 Peter 3:14)?
Application: How does the expectation of new heavens and a new earth shape your priorities today? What 'spots or blemishes' do you need to address in your life?

subsections.title: Final Exhortations
subsections.content: Peter commends Paul's writings and closes with a call to grow in grace.

questions.question: Context: Why does Peter reference Paul's letters here? What might some have done with Paul's teaching?

Observation: How should the Lord's patience be counted (2 Peter 3:15)? What does Peter say about Paul's letters (2 Peter 3:15-16)? What do 'the ignorant and unstable' do with Paul's writings (2 Peter 3:16)? What warning does Peter give (2 Peter 3:17)? What command does he close with (2 Peter 3:18)?

Meaning: What does Peter's reference to Paul's writings 'in all his letters' (2 Peter 3:16) tell us about the emerging New Testament canon? What are 'the other Scriptures' Paul's letters are grouped with (2 Peter 3:16)? What does it mean to 'twist' the Scriptures 'to their own destruction' (2 Peter 3:16)? How do we 'grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ' (2 Peter 3:18)?
Application: How can you guard against being 'carried away with the error of lawless people' (2 Peter 3:17)? What does 'growing in grace and knowledge' look like practically in your life?

subsections.title: Study Summary
subsections.content:
Key Themes of 2 Peter:

  • Precious Promises — God's divine power has granted all we need for life and godliness (1:3-4)
  • Confirm Your Calling — Supplement faith with virtue; make your calling and election sure (1:5-11)
  • Scripture's Authority — Prophecy came not by human will but by men carried along by the Holy Spirit (1:20-21)
  • False Teachers — Destructive heresies, denying the Master, exploiting with false words (2:1-3)
  • God's Justice — God knows how to rescue the godly and reserve the unrighteous for judgment (2:9)
  • The Day of the Lord — Coming like a thief; patient, not slow, that all should come to repentance (3:8-10)
  • New Creation — New heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (3:13)
  • Growing in Grace — Grow in grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ (3:18)

To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. (2 Peter 3:18)
